topic: Squares, a parabola and the greatest common divisor
script: Here is a quick tour of three small ideas from mathematics. First, a pattern in square numbers. Six squared is thirty six. And thirty six is also the sum of the first six odd numbers. Every square number can be built this way, one odd number at a time, like the layers of a growing square. Next, the shape of squaring. If we draw y equals x squared, we get a curve called a parabola. It falls to zero at the middle and rises on both sides. The curve is perfectly symmetric, because a number and its negative have the same square. Finally, an algorithm that is more than two thousand years old. Euclid found the greatest common divisor of two numbers by repeated remainders. Start with forty eight and eighteen. Forty eight divided by eighteen leaves twelve. Eighteen divided by twelve leaves six. Twelve divided by six leaves nothing at all. So the greatest common divisor is six. Each step is simple, and the answer is always exact. Because every remainder is smaller than the number before it, the method can never run forever. That is why computers still use Euclid's idea today, more than two thousand years after he wrote it down.
